entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

The next war doesn't necessarily begin with the firing of the first missile. Before that, a battle is already underway — over truth, over assigning blame, over legitimizing military action. Who broke the agreement? Who started the conflict? Who will bear responsibility for the consequences of the next war? The answers to these questions may be constructed and locked in on the media battlefield before the military conflict even begins.

Take the narrative that has taken shape in recent days around attacks on oil tankers and commercial ships: that Iran deliberately violated the Islamabad Understanding and is therefore responsible for the collapse of the agreement and the possible escalation of war. That the attacks occurred is one thing; turning that into a definitive narrative of Iran's unilateral responsibility — without examining the obligations of the parties, the US naval blockade, and the sequence of military actions — is another. Sometimes, to build a misleading narrative, there's no need to fabricate reality at all; it's enough to select part of the truth and omit the rest.

We have seen this before, too, in attempts to discredit real images of the bombing of Tehran. Some media accounts claimed the images of destruction were staged and that the women seen in the photos were actresses who kept reappearing. An independent review of the images from Sabounchi Street in Tehran refuted that claim. Here, the issue wasn't merely the publication of a false news item; it was an attempt to make the audience doubt reality itself, even when confronted with documented images of destruction and war victims.

In the possible next stage of the war, we must be more vigilant than ever against three phenomena: Misinformation — false information spread unknowingly; Disinformation — fake and distorted information deliberately produced to deceive; and Malinformation — real information used to cause harm, for example by revealing the identity or location of individuals at risk. These three can be deployed simultaneously to sow panic, destroy public trust, deny the realities of war, and prepare public opinion to accept a new conflict.

In such conditions, the war propaganda headquarters, if it exists, must monitor the information space moment by moment and respond with speed, accuracy, and verifiable evidence. Of course, countering information warfare doesn't mean constructing counter-narratives or denying unpleasant realities. The main capital in this battle is public trust, and that capital is preserved only through honesty and transparency.

The war of narratives may, before the military war, produce one crucial outcome: whom the public considers the initiator of the war, whom it recognizes as the victim, and whom it holds responsible for the destruction that follows.

The report "Regulatory Oversight of Environmental Water Rights Allocation under Table (7) of Article (37) of the Seventh Development Plan Law," prepared by Mehdi Rajabi and Ali Haji-Moradi in Shahrivar 1405, examines the gap between legal commitments and the actual delivery of water needed by ecosystems.

The report's findings for the water year 1403–1404 show that drought is not the only reason water rights are not being fulfilled; weaknesses in the allocation system, withdrawals along the route, lack of coordination among agencies, and the absence of transparent monitoring also play a role.

The report's central message is clear: releasing water from a dam alone does not mean environmental water rights have been secured. The evaluation criterion must be whether water reaches the target ecosystem, in a volume, quality, and timing suited to its needs.

The report emphasizes reforming water allocation under water-scarce conditions, online monitoring and public disclosure of data, controlling withdrawals along the route, and integrated management of river basins.

🌱 Environmental water rights must hold a stable place in water allocation decisions — a share whose provision does not depend on water left over after other uses.

It always seemed to me that if this transformation took place in the seminaries, it would be more beneficial for society. But I returned unsuccessful. In the year 1372, after much pressure, I came and bought a house in Tehran and returned to Tehran to live. Again some of the gentlemen insisted that no, stay in the seminary. In his autobiography, the late Arthur Arberry writes of the late Reynold A. Nicholson — scholar, commentator, and translator of literary and mystical works from Persian and Arabic into English:

He was a consummate scholar, so enamored of his books that he sacrificed his eyesight to ceaseless reading, so humble and self-effacing that he had no idea of his own greatness. In the final years of his life, when the lamp of his eyes was flickering toward extinction, he composed this verse — a poem that, to me, among all the last words ever uttered by human beings, carries the truest inspiration and the most moving farewell:

When Truth appears unveiled before your eyes,
These tongues are left bewildered and surprised.
*I shall fall silent — the Beloved has come to speak:*
*Listen, and God knows best what is right and true.*
*Become devoid of sense, of hearing, and of thought,*
*That you may hear the summons "Return!"*
As long as this tongue remains, you shall not hear the Word.
So words must be brief. And peace.

**I have borrowed the Persian rendering of Nicholson's poem from verses of the Masnavi. The asterisked lines are from the Masnavi.

- Nicholson's poem, as narrated by Arberry, reads:
When Truth shines out words fail and nothing tell;
Now hear the Voice within your hearts. Farewell.

This is the closing verse of a long poem that Arberry quoted and confirmed earlier in this same piece, noting that in these verses Nicholson was deeply influenced by Rumi: ... He seldom spoke of his personal beliefs, and I, too, in twenty-five years of close friendship with him, learned little about how he was raised or of his spiritual journey. Yet the image that took shape in my mind was that he, like many others, had lost his faith in youth and then recovered it through intellectual companionship and kinship of spirit with Muslim mystics.

In his old age, he composed a poem in which, for the first time, he laid bare his innermost thoughts. It was clear that these thoughts had been profoundly shaped by long years of studying Rumi's works ...

Sometimes we look at the past and say: If I had spent those years doing something else, I would have a better life today. Why did I play so much as a child? Why did I pursue things in my youth that no longer matter to me today?

Every way of life opens up possibilities before us and also carries costs. We cannot compare our lived life with an imaginary life that has all the good things and pays no price for them.

▪️ Let us seize the remaining opportunities

Not all opportunities are lost with the end of youth. There are still things we can begin, things we can learn, and pleasures we can experience.

If we spend today only on regret for yesterday, in a few more years, today will also become a new subject for regret.

The cost of chartering a supertanker from the Persian Gulf to Asia has hit $1.2 million, insurance has gotten more expensive, and ships carrying fertilizer, aluminum, petrochemicals, and grain are still stranded in the Persian Gulf. America has sent a third aircraft carrier to the region, and its navy is, according to experts, stretched thin.
The drawdown from reserves is also heavy: 400 million barrels drawn from reserves in March, another 100 million barrels from the G7, America's strategic reserves at their lowest level since 1983, and JPMorgan saying it sees no end to this situation.
In other words, Iran can't fully close the strait, and America can't fully open it. Unless Trump reaches a deal with Iran; that's what the market is really waiting for.
Why is this news encouraging for us?
1. Trump's leverage has hit its ceiling. With three aircraft carriers, the strait has only become "half-open." When American experts themselves say the only way out is a deal with Iran, it means the military option costs more than it delivers.
2. The clock is working against the White House. The November midterm elections are approaching, and according to experts, fuel prices won't come down by then; the soaring cost of diesel has even hit American farmers. This pressure raises the incentive for a deal. But it's clear that the cost of this war is being paid by the people of Iran.
3. A deal would untie many knots at once. A world whose reserves have run dry is thirsty for fresh supply; it's not just oil — petrochemicals, fertilizer, and metals are also stuck behind this barrier.
The world has come to believe that Hormuz today is neither closed nor open; and the key is not on warships but on the negotiating table.

✅ According to a report from one of the well-known publishers and bookstores, the best-selling book in Tehran's bookstores over the past few months has been Ferdowsi's Shahnameh. ✅ Perhaps this phenomenon cannot be explained merely by literary interest or a growing desire to read the Shahnameh. 🔴 Why do even good things sometimes make us feel bad? ✍️ Mostafa Malekian

We usually assume that if good things happen to us, we'll feel good too. But the pleasantness of an event, in itself, doesn't guarantee that we can handle it well.

We live in a world that can be hard on us in two ways: not everything goes the way we want, and we have no certainty about what's coming.

▪️ The world has no obligation to fulfill our desires

There's no reason all the world's events should conform to our preferences and wishes. Some events are pleasant and some unpleasant; even a single event can make one person happy and another miserable.

Rain is a source of joy for a farmer waiting to water his field; but for a launderer who has hung washed clothes out to dry in the sun, it spells trouble.

The rain is the same rain; what differs is its relation to our desires and circumstances. The world has neither sworn to be our enemy nor promised to always go along with what we want.

▪️ Even joys may show up uninvited

The difficulty isn't just that we dislike certain events; it's also that we don't know what will come, or when.

Suppose you love someone dearly, but they show up at your door unannounced. Despite being happy to see them, you might lose your composure and fail to receive them the way you'd like.

Loving a guest is not the same as being ready for their arrival.

The same holds for the good things in life: we may want something, yet not be prepared for its sudden arrival. As a result, our reaction may be ill-considered and create fresh problems.

▪️ The suffering of the event and the suffering of the reaction

Part of life's difficulty comes from events not matching our desires; another part can stem from how we face them.

If we expect life to always unfold according to our wishes and predictions, we'll be constantly caught off guard. And being caught off guard can push us into reactions that only deepen our suffering.

So we must prepare ourselves to live in a world that holds both adversity and uncertainty—so that we can meet what arrives uninvited with greater composure.

We can't control the arrival of every uninvited guest; but we can learn how to face them.

For complex human problems, we shouldn't be looking for technical answers! If a pipe in your house bursts, that's a technical problem; but when your neighbor puts their trash out earlier than they're supposed to, that's no longer merely technical — it belongs to the realm of human problems. In teaching problem-solving, the first thing we draw the learner's attention to is distinguishing the technical problem from the human problem, and when we talk about problem-solving and teaching it, we mean the second category — because technical problems require expertise in their own field. If my phone stops working, I go to a specialist and they fix it. But human problems don't necessarily have predetermined solutions, and technical expertise alone won't help solve them. The solution to these problems has to be discovered, and solving them requires a basic understanding of the humanities and learning the skill of problem-solving. The biggest mistake is usually offering technical solutions for problems with human roots. When my employees' motivation is low and they show up late to work because of it, I can't force them into line with punishment, incentives, and a few new rules; I need to ask why their motivation has dropped, invite them into a conversation, and address the problem at the level of human relationships. Another mistake is assuming that our technical expertise can help us solve human problems — which it absolutely cannot. Yet another mistake is framing problems with human roots in technical terms. In that same example of lateness, if I say the reason is that they wake up late and that a morning phone call will get them to work on time, I've framed a human problem in technical terms! Mistaking technical problems for human ones and vice versa, offering technical solutions for human problems, and expecting clear technical solutions for complex problems — these are among the greatest plagues of our country's decision-making and problem-solving system. New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools

In the second half of the 1990s, some households, arguing that schools were not religious enough, pulled their children out of school and created a form of home-schooling. The COVID-19 outbreak further entrenched this situation, albeit on a very limited scale. Out of this current, mosque-schools gradually took shape; first established in Qom, they grew rapidly, and today they have branches in 22 provinces and operate under a central headquarters. The number of these schools has doubled over the past 4 years, surpassing 450; with an average of about 30 students per school. After several years of operation, these schools finally obtained operating licenses starting in 1402 as a type of non-governmental school, and they also signed agreements with the government to expand into rural areas. Because these schools use mosque facilities, their tuition is lower, and in addition to more religious instruction, they offer skill-training and income-generation programs; especially income generation through cyberspace and cryptocurrencies.

Alongside this current, a trend of establishing home-schools has also begun in Tehran and is rapidly growing. These are also schools with a student body of between 20 and 40, with very high tuition, often run with supplementary curricula and in more private settings. Many of these home-schools are in practice smaller branches of a private school or affiliated with one. Despite the Ministry of Education's current opposition, these schools do not conflict with the general logic of policymaking in the ministry and face no obstacle to expansion. Home-schools are in the early stages of consolidation, and their activities have so far been reported in some areas of Tehran as well as the metropolises of Tabriz and Isfahan.

The expansion of these micro-schools signals the continuation and intensification of differentiation and the ever-increasing stratification of parts of society into smaller units; a kind of intra-group and intra-class fragmentation. Mosque-schools represent a form of differentiation among more religious families themselves, just as home-schools represent further differentiation among the upper strata of society. These schools should not be conflated with diversity in the educational system, because educational diversity is positive only when it is accompanied by universal access and the possibility of genuine choice for all social groups. New micro-schools: mosque-schools and home-schools

In the second half of the 1990s, some households, arguing that schools were not religious enough, pulled their children out of school and created a form of home-schooling. The COVID-19 outbreak further entrenched this arrangement, albeit on a very limited scale. Out of this current, mosque-schools gradually took shape; first established in Qom, they multiplied rapidly and today have branches in 22 provinces, overseen by a central headquarters. Over the past 4 years, the number of these schools has more than doubled to over 450, with an average of roughly 30 students per school. After several years of operation, these schools were finally granted operating licenses starting in 1402 as a type of non-governmental school, and they also signed agreements with the government to expand into rural areas. Because these schools use mosque facilities, their tuition is lower, and beyond more extensive religious instruction, they also offer skills training and income-generation programs—particularly income generation through cyberspace and cryptocurrencies.

Alongside this current, a trend of establishing home-schools has also emerged, starting in Tehran and growing rapidly. These too are schools with a student body of between 20 and 40, charging very high tuition, and are often run with supplementary curricula in more private settings. Many of these home-schools are in practice smaller branches of, or affiliated with, a private school. Despite the Ministry of Education's current opposition, these schools do not conflict with the ministry's overall policy logic and face no obstacle to expansion. Home-schools are in the early stages of becoming established, and their activities have so far been reported in some areas of Tehran as well as the metropolises of Tabriz and Isfahan.

The spread of these micro-schools signals the continuation and intensification of differentiation and the ever-increasing stratification of parts of society into smaller units—a kind of intra-group and intra-class fragmentation. Mosque-schools represent a form of differentiation among more religious families themselves, just as home-schools represent further differentiation among the upper strata of society. These schools should not be conflated with diversity in the educational system, because educational diversity is positive only when it is accompanied by universal access and the possibility of genuine choice for all social groups. Although these schools currently account for a negligible share of the educational system, they are significant in terms of institutional analysis.@Omidi_Reza
